claim: A 'loop' is defined by practitioners as an autonomous, self-correcting feedback cycle where an AI agent repeatedly acts, tests its results, and adjusts its approach until a specific goal is met.
stance_target: definition of agentic loops for continuous operation architecture (Pillar 5)
quoted_support: A loop is an autonomous, self-correcting feedback cycle where an AI agent repeatedly acts, tests its results and adjusts its approach until a specific goal is met.

claim: Claude Code's /goal primitive uses an independent evaluator model that checks a user-defined, deterministic stopping condition each time the agent tries to stop, preventing the agent from self-judging 'good enough.'
stance_target: rigid evals architecture for zero-hallucination quality control (Pillar 1)
quoted_support: Each time Claude tries to stop, an evaluator model checks your condition and sends it back to work until the goal is met or a number of turns you define is reached. This is why deterministic criteria, such as number of tests passed or clearing a certain score threshold, are so effective.

claim: Claude Code's team defines four loop types by trigger/stop mechanism: manual (agentic, human-directed per turn), goal-based (/goal, evaluator-checked), time-based (/loop, fixed interval, session-scoped), and proactive/scheduled (/schedule, event-driven, cloud-run with no real-time human).
stance_target: triggers and continuous operation taxonomy for the software factory (Pillar 5)
scope_conditions: Claude Code official taxonomy as summarized by practitioner, 2026
quoted_support: We categorize a few different types of loops based on: how they are triggered, how they are stopped, what Claude Code primitive is used, what type of task is most appropriate for each.

claim: Recurring /loop tasks in Claude Code expire seven days after creation and are session-scoped, stopping when a new conversation starts unless resumed with --resume or --continue; tasks needing to outlive a session require /schedule (cloud execution).
stance_target: infrastructure constraints on continuous agentic operation (Pillar 5)
quoted_support: Recurring loops expire seven days after creation... loops are session-scoped, so they stop when you start a new conversation - though resuming that session with --resume or --continue brings back any recurring task still inside its seven-day window. If you need something that outlives your session, /schedule runs it in the cloud.

claim: A core verification discipline for agentic loops is that the agent which performed the work must not be the sole judge of whether the work is good; a separate agent (or the human) must verify it.
scope_conditions: practitioner lesson learned from a near-miss incident
quoted_support: The other habit that matters here is not letting the agent that did the work decide the work is good. One sub-agent drafts the change. A separate one verifies it.

claim: A documented production use case: an 80,000+-star open-source repository receiving 80-90 pull requests per day is triaged via an hourly /loop that checks GitHub for new issues/PRs and summarizes urgency, reducing manual daily review burden.
stance_target: feasibility of event-driven continuous operation for real engineering workloads (Pillar 5)
scope_conditions: Addy Osmani's Agent Skills open-source repository, 2026
quoted_support: We've got over 80,000 stars, and up until recently we were getting anywhere up to like 80 or 90 pull requests that we had to review a day... Now with loop, what you can do is say: well, every 24 hours or every 12 hours, check the GitHub repository for any new open issues and provide a summary of their urgency.

claim: Loop engineering is a poor fit for tasks with vague, subjective, or open-ended creative success criteria, because the evaluator can only check hard, deterministic rules against the transcript, not quality or taste.
stance_target: applying autonomous loops universally across all software factory department tasks (Pillar 2/5)
scope_conditions: general applicability limits of goal/loop primitives
quoted_support: Tasks that require human taste, subjective design, or open-ended creative exploration aren't a good fit. The evaluator sitting behind goal... doesn't look at the content to see if it's good or bad in any way, shape, or form. All it does is examine the conversation transcript to see if the hard rules you specified have been met.

claim: A practitioner heuristic for detecting a stuck/malfunctioning loop: if the same command is retried a third time with no change in result, it is probably time to stop the loop.
quoted_support: One classic sign that you've got a loop spinning in place is the same command being tried over and over without any change in the result. Give the same command a third time with no change from the second and it's probably time to stop.
